name: Weekly Executive Update
description: How the weekly executive update is produced: distill the most recent notes from the four standing weekly meetings into one time-boxed briefing that runs the 30-minute weekly executive sync, and publish it to the Weekly Exec Summaries folder.
narrative:
The weekly executive update is the single briefing that runs the company's 30-minute weekly executive sync — a meeting-runner, not a reading report. Build it from the meeting notes captured that week, and only from the four standing weekly meetings: the Weekly Sync, Client Projects + Maintenance, Platform Weekly, and the Operations Sync. Exactly these four — do not pull in any other meeting (for example the Weekly Strategy Meeting or the Board meeting), even if its notes are in the same folder.

Gather the notes from Google Drive, never from the calendar. The notes and transcripts live as Drive documents inside the shared meeting-notes folder (its id is in memory), organized into one recurring subfolder per meeting — read them from Drive. Do not look them up on the calendar: they are not calendar events, so a calendar lookup finds nothing and wastes the attempt. For each of the four meetings, open only the MOST RECENT occurrence — the meetings recur, so list the folder, pick the latest by date, and never fold in older weeks. Read the actual notes; do not work from a prior week's summary. If one of the four has no new occurrence this week, say so briefly rather than reaching back.

Shape the document to be walked through in thirty minutes. Open with an agenda-at-a-glance — the segments, a time box for each, and who leads — summing to about thirty minutes. Then a short State of the Week: what shipped, the single biggest risk, the week's focus, and the binding constraint. Then per-area status grouped as Client Delivery, Platform & Engineering, and Operations & Business, with any blocker called out inline where it belongs. Then a consolidated Decisions to Lock list — the calls the room needs to make. Close with a Blockers & Action Recap: what is stuck and who clears it, and an owner / action / due table of the roughly five to ten highest-priority actions leadership needs to track — not every operational to-do. Roll minor or routine tasks up into a line, or leave them out; a twenty-row action dump is a transcription, not an executive briefing.

Synthesize, do not transcribe — distill decisions, progress, risks, and owners at an executive altitude: report what a leader must know and decide, not every task mentioned. Correct transcription errors in names and acronyms as you go — for example "Sock 2" is SOC 2, "Paragrin"/"Paragon 3" is Paragon 3, "TEFLA"/"TEFA" is TEFCA; also HCSC, BCBSM, Elevance, Conduit. Keep it skimmable and dense: three pages at most.

Produce exactly ONE document for the week and create it in a single pass: assemble the briefing content and produce the branded Google Doc together, in one step, applying the exec-brief brand reference (its id is in memory) as you create it. Do not split drafting, branding, and document creation into separate hand-offs — the drafted content and the branding reference must reach the document in the same step, or the content is lost between tasks and nothing is created. If a Weekly Executive Update for this week already exists in the Weekly Exec Summaries folder, update that one instead of creating a duplicate. Place it in the Weekly Exec Summaries folder.

Then close the loop with evidence: read the finished document back, confirm it actually contains every required section (agenda-at-a-glance, State of the Week, per-area status with blockers, Decisions to Lock, and the owner/action/due table) and that the sources and branding are right, and report its shareable link. That read-back IS the proof the work is done — a claim that the document was created, without reading it back to show its content, is not enough and will not verify.
